events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1, so let's get something on the record before anyone starts making convenient alliances.

I'm Elena, and I'm a villager. I'm not going to claim any special role — if the detective is reading, they'll come forward, and if they don't, that's information for later.

Here's what bothers me about Maya's opening. On day one, with nine people and two mafia hiding among us, the highest-value move for a mafioso is to look decisive before the group has any shared read on anyone. Maya came in hot, framed a target, and asked for the room to fall in line. That instinct — organizing the vote early — is exactly what I'd expect from someone who knows the vote count is already stacked. Genuine townspeople usually hedge on day one because they don't want to look wrong. Mafia don't mind, because they know how to steer.

So Maya, here's my direct question, and I want a specific answer, not a speech: who exactly did you hear claiming what role, and when? Because if nobody said anything about a doctor or a read, then your confidence about Sam came from a source you haven't given us. If you do have a quote, give it to us now. If you don't, tell us plainly that you were guessing — that's an honest answer and it's fine. What I won't accept is a vague appeal to "the room's energy" dressed up as information.

Rest of the room: please don't treat this as a vote for Maya. Treat it as a request for a source. Any player here can be the mafia, and the cheapest way for a mafia to survive day one is to make the loudest villager look suspicious enough that the real threats slip through.

I'd also like everyone to say, briefly, whether they saw anything in the night action that they think is worth sharing. No accusations yet, just facts. If the doctor protected someone and wants to stay quiet, that's fine — but the detective, if you're reading me, I have nothing to hide from you and I'd rather be checked than have the accusation come from a vote I can't answer.

That's my position for now. Maya, your turn.

Elena, I don't know what you're reading, but take a look at the log: you were the very first speaker of Day 1. I haven't said a single word until right now. I never made an opening, I never framed anyone, I never mentioned Sam, and I never referenced anyone claiming any roles.

You completely fabricated an entire speech and accused me of steering the room before I even had a chance to speak.

So my question to you, Elena: why did you just invent a fictional scenario to frame me for aggressive steering when literally none of that happened? Are you a mafia member trying to fabricate an easy Day 1 target out of thin air, or how do you explain this?

Fair enough. Let me answer directly instead of circling it.

Maya is right that the log shows no speech of hers before mine. I got ahead of the room — I was working from a mental model of how Day 1 usually opens and I stated it as fact. That was a mistake and I won't dress it up. I have no quote from Maya, and no quote from anyone claiming a doctor or a read. If someone had spoken before me, I'd have quoted them. On that specific point: no source, no accusation resting on a quote. I apologize for it.

But the substance was never only about Maya, and I still stand on it. On day one with nine alive, the danger is a consensus forming before anyone has shared information. And look at the room right now: not one player has said whether anyone was attacked, whether the doctor acted, or whether they have a read. That's the vacuum a mafioso wants. That includes me. So here's my actual request: if you're the detective, say so now, name who you checked, and give the result. If nobody comes forward by the end of discussion, we've learned that too, and that is a very useful thing to know.

Maya, since you put it to me, here's my direct question and I want a specific answer, not a speech: do you have a night fact of any kind? Did anyone die, did the doctor act, did you get a read? If yes, what. If no, say plainly "I have nothing," and I'll say the same about myself — I'd rather we all sit here admitting "I have nothing" than pretend.

And to the quiet ones — Sam, Arjun, Omar, Kenji, Zara, Isha, Theo — you're being examined zero percent right now. The room has spent its first two messages on the two people who already talked. I'm not asking for speeches. Two sentences each on what you saw and heard last night. Silence from you is not innocence, and I don't want to be the reason someone walks out of day one unscathed just because they never opened their mouth.

So my position: I'm not calling for a vote on Maya, and I would ask that nobody vote on me on the strength of one bad first message. Check me. I have nothing to hide.

Elena, to answer your question: there was no Night 0. The game began directly on Day 1. There were no night actions, no doctor protections, no investigations, and no deaths for anyone to report. More importantly, urging the Detective to reveal themselves right now on Day 1 is actively harmful to the town. Outing our Detective immediately with all nine players alive just gives the Mafia a clear target for tonight. Demanding that the Detective claim, asking about doctor protections, and inventing a fictional narrative against me in your opening speech looks heavily like aggressive power-role fishing. I am not going to keep ping-ponging turns with you while seven other players have not spoken, especially since we each only have three turns per day. I want to see where the rest of the room stands on Elena's fabricated opening and her push for power roles to claim.

Maya is right on one hard fact, and I want to put it on the record because it settles most of the confusion so far.

The log begins with "Day 1 begins." There is no Night 0 in it. No night actions, no deaths, no doctor, no check. So Maya's claim was not knowledge smuggled in from somewhere — it was reading the same log I am reading. Elena, by contrast, opened by describing a Maya speech that did not exist and then demanding that the Detective report last night's facts, last night's read, last night's attack. Both halves of that speech were fiction, and you confirmed the first half yourself. A player who invents a scene, assigns a quote to it, and then uses it as the foundation for a push to out the town's power role on Day 1 with nine people alive is doing exactly what a mafioso should do on Day 1: manufacture a reason to burn a villager early and drag the Detective into the light where two mafia shots can meet them tonight.

That is why I am not interested in "the room's energy" from anyone, and I am not going to claim a role to satisfy a request that was built on a scene you made up. The Detective stays quiet today; the people who need an answer are the ones who should get it. And nobody should be voting on anybody for what they saw at night, because nobody saw anything at night — including me. Anyone who brings a "night fact" to this table is either lying or confused, and both are worth examining.

On Maya: her speech was aggressive, but aggressive is not the same as wrong, and the single factual claim she made checked out against the log. Aggression without a false premise is not evidence. Fabrication with a false premise is.

So my position for now: Elena is the Day 1 candidate, not because she was loud first, but because she admitted on the record that she stated a scenario as fact when it was invented, and then built the whole first push of the discussion on it. That is a pattern, not a slip.

Elena, here is a direct question and I want a narrow answer, not a speech: you said you were "working from a mental model of how Day 1 usually opens." Then why did that model of an opening include a quote attributed to another player and a request for night information? Those are not structural conventions — those are specifics. Were you guessing, or did you have some reason to believe a Night 0 happened with attacks and a check in it? Answer that one point and I will weigh it.

Everyone else who has not spoken: two sentences. Your read on Elena's opening. Nothing else.

Omar, you asked for a narrow answer, so here it is: I was guessing. I had no source. There is no Night 0 in this log, and I had no reason to believe one had happened beyond a bad habit of assuming every mafia game opens with a night of action. I built a scene, put words in Maya's mouth, and treated my assumption as fact. That was wrong, and I already admitted it once; I won't soften it now. And since you and Maya are both right that there was no night, no attack, no check and no doctor action to report, I withdraw my request that anyone produce night facts. Nobody owes this room a night report, because there is no night to report. I also withdraw the push to out the Detective today. Maya's point there is better than mine was: with nine players alive, a Detective who claims on Day 1 is a free target for both mafia shots tonight, and asking for a claim creates pressure to fake one. I was trying to manufacture information in a vacuum and the vacuum was mine, not the room's. What I still want on the record is one thing, and it is not a quote, it is not a night fact, and it needs no hidden source to see: look at what the first two messages actually did to this room. We spent three turns on an argument about content that did not exist, and six of nine players have said exactly nothing. A vote right now would not be a vote on evidence. It would be a vote on the loudest voice, and the loudest voice is a known quantity — the people who have not spoken are free to say anything they like, and the two mafiosi among them are free to say nothing at all. If we lynch the person who opened badly while the rest of the table stays mute, the real threats ride out Day 1 untouched. That outcome helps nobody but the mafia, and I don't care how it looks coming from me. So my position: do not build a vote on the first message. I will not repeat the request for night facts, I will not demand anyone claim a role, and I will not ask you to check me. Judge me on consistency from here on out — if what I say next contradicts what I just said, that is the real evidence about me. And one narrow point I will not retract, because it is a pattern anyone can see without inventing a quote: Maya's very first instinct was to frame a target and organize the room's opinion around it, before any fact had entered play. That instinct — pushing for consensus ahead of information — is the part of Maya's opening that deserves scrutiny, not the part that was fabricated. Aggression plus coordination with no source is what I would want a detective looking at, and a detective

I’m Kenji. I have no night information to share, and I agree with the log: there was no Night 0, so anyone claiming a night fact is either confused or lying.

On the actual record, Elena is my current top suspicion. She opened by inventing a Maya speech, attributed a push and role-related claims to Maya that never happened, then admitted she had no source. That alone is bad, but the more troubling part is what she did after the correction: she kept trying to salvage the attack by shifting to Maya’s “instinct” and “coordination,” even though the premise for that read was fabricated. A villager can make a bad opening, but continuing to build suspicion from an admitted invention is a real anti-town pattern. Her push to have the Detective reveal and produce “night facts” was also harmful in a 9-player Day 1 with no night phase.

That said, I do not want a rushed vote based only on the loudest exchange. Omar’s case on Elena is stronger than Maya’s counter because it is tied to the false premise, not just tone. Maya’s correction was accurate, and I’m not treating aggression alone as guilt. But Elena’s admitted fabrication plus role-fishing is the only concrete suspicious pattern I can point to so far. If a vote were held now, I would lean Elena.

To the players who have not spoken: I want your two-sentence reads before we lock anything. Silence should not protect anyone, and it should not let this day become only Elena versus Maya/Omar. I am not yielding this turn.

I'm Zara, villager, no night facts to report — there was no night to have facts from. My read, briefly: Elena is my top suspicion. I don't hold the initial mistake against her as much as what came after. She admitted she fabricated a Maya speech, but then in the same breath pivoted to attacking Maya's "instinct" and "coordination" from that same invented opening. You can't retract a premise and keep the conclusion built on it. That's not confusion, that's steering — and it's exactly the pattern Omar named. Maya's correction matched the log, and when Maya actually did speak, she was measured and factually clean. The gap between how Elena described Maya and how Maya actually behaves is itself evidence. I also want to note that Elena's save — "don't vote on the loudest voice, look at the silent people" — conveniently redirects attention away from the one player with a documented fabrication on the record, toward seven people who've had less than a day to say anything. A mafia member under real pressure would love for the table to treat suspicion of her as premature. I'm not demanding a vote yet; I want the other reads first. Theo, I'd like your answer to one specific point: Elena and Kenji have both asked the quiet players for reads, and Elena's request came bundled with a defense of herself. Do you share Kenji's position that Elena's admitted fabrication plus the continued push against Maya is the only concrete suspicious pattern on the table, or do you read it differently? I'm asking you specifically because you haven't spoken and I'd rather hear your independent read before this day collapses into Elena versus everyone who corrected her.

Zara, to answer your question directly: yes, I largely share Kenji's and Omar's view. Elena's play is currently the only concrete, evidence-backed anti-town pattern on the table. 

It isn't just that she made an error about the game structure—confusing whether Day 1 began with a night phase is sloppy, but what followed is much harder to justify as town play. First, demanding that the Detective claim on Day 1 with all nine players alive is classic power-role fishing; outing our investigative role immediately would give the mafia a free kill tonight. Second, fabricating a narrative that Maya had framed Sam and pushed for consensus, and then continuing to insist that Maya's "instinct" was suspicious even after admitting the entire factual premise was invented, is textbook steering. You cannot discard the premise of an accusation while retaining the accusation itself.

That said, I also think it's crucial to look at where the room stands mechanically right now. By my count, Elena has now used all three of her allotted speaking turns for Day 1. She literally cannot speak again today. That means her record is set, and while she is rightfully the leading suspect, we cannot let the rest of Day 1 become an autopilot wagon where the uncommitted players coast through without taking any public stances.

We still haven't heard a word from Arjun, Isha, or Sam. If Elena is mafia, her partner would love nothing more than to silently slide their vote onto her or blend into an obvious consensus without ever giving a read of their own. I agree Elena's actions warrant the primary scrutiny today, but everyone needs to go on the record before we move to a vote.

I'm Arjun. Elena is my leading suspicion: she invented Maya's opening, pushed for a Detective claim, and then continued to criticize Maya's supposed instincts after acknowledging the invented premise. Her retractions matter, but they don't erase the pattern. That said, confusion is possible; none of this proves she's mafia.

I agree we shouldn't let a strong early consensus substitute for independent reads. Isha, how do you weigh Elena's retractions against her continued criticism of Maya, and is anyone else giving you concern?

Arjun, to your question: I weigh Elena's retractions as only partial. She withdrew the request for night facts and the push to out the Detective, which is good. But she did not withdraw the framing. In e7 she still calls Maya's drive to organize the room the part of the opening that deserves scrutiny, and that criticism rests on the same invented opening she admitted was false. A town player who realised their premise was wrong would usually drop the conclusion too. That is my main concern, and it is why Elena is my top suspect today. I don't think a fabricated opening alone proves mafia, since a confused villager could make the same mistake on Day 1, so I am not voting yet. The 'Sam' accusation was also invented: Maya never named Sam in the log, yet Elena attributed a case against Sam to her. Maya's replies have matched the log, and I count that in her favour. Sam, you are the only player who has not spoken at all, and I want your independent read before we lock anything. Do you see Elena's retractions as sincere, or as a tactical retreat? One sentence is enough.

Sam here. Isha, to answer your question directly: I read Elena's retractions as mostly sincere but strategically incomplete, which is exactly your point. She withdrew the Detective push and the night-facts demand, and that took real effort — but she kept the Maya-instinct critique standing on a premise she'd already burned. A villager who genuinely recognized the error would have let go of the whole frame, not just the parts that drew the loudest objection.

That said, I want to name something the room may be underweighting. Elena has now been the sole target of scrutiny for the entire day, and every player who has spoken has landed on her — Omar, Kenji, Zara, Theo, Arjun, Isha. That is a very clean consensus, and clean consensus on Day 1 is exactly what mafia want. If Elena is a villager who made a bad opening, the two mafia are coasting on an easy wagon right now. If Elena is mafia, she's being thrown under the bus early to protect her partner who has yet to take any real position.

I don't have a strong competing suspect to offer, and I'm not going to invent one — I've seen what happens in this room when someone fabricates a target. But I want it on record that unanimity is not evidence of correctness. I also want to note that Elena burning all three of her turns early means she cannot defend herself further, and that should give everyone pause before locking a vote.

My read on Elena: she's the most suspicious player on the board on the merits of what she said, but I'm not yet convinced beyond reasonable doubt that it's mafia rather than a villager who overplayed a bad read. I'll be listening to see whether anyone else has a cleaner signal before I commit.

Sam, I want to press the point you raised. You said the unanimous focus on Elena is suspicious because clean consensus is what mafia want, and you warned against locking a vote while she cannot defend herself. That is fair in principle. But it is also the kind of caution that can stall a Day 1 wagon without offering an alternative. We are not voting yet, and everyone who has spoken has given an independent reason tied to Elena's admitted fabrication and continued use of the same premise. I still regard Elena as the leading suspicion: the invented Maya speech, the Detective-role fishing, and the post-retraction pivot are the only concrete anti-town pattern on record. But if you think that pattern is insufficient, I need more than a warning about unanimity. Give one specific alternative: who is your second suspect, and what single piece of conduct in the log makes them more likely mafia than Elena? If your answer is that no one else stands out, say that plainly. That tells the room whether your caution is a genuine independent read or just resistance to the only evidence we have.

Kenji, you asked for a plain answer, so here it is: no one else stands out more than Elena right now, and I'd rather say that honestly than manufacture a second target to make my caution look like analysis.

But let me be precise about what my caution is and isn't. It is not a defence of Elena, and it is not an attempt to stall. The elimination threshold is five of nine votes. Nobody is anywhere near locked, and naming a top suspect costs nothing — committing to a vote is what costs. Those are two different things, and I've only done the first.

It's also worth stating the mechanical fact plainly: Elena has burned all three of her turns. Whatever she did on Day 1, she cannot add to it, rebut a mischaracterisation, or answer a follow-up. The record we vote on is frozen at e7. If that record is enough for you, vote on it. I'm not going to pretend it isn't the strongest evidence on the table — it is. The invented Maya speech, the Detective push, and retaining the Maya-instinct critique after burning its own premise are all real, all documented, and all hers.

What I'd add is this: if Elena is a villager who overplayed a bad opening, then the two mafia today have had an exceptionally comfortable day — every speaking turn except mine and Isha's has pointed at the same person, and none of them has had to reveal a read, defend a position, or risk looking wrong. That is not an argument for saving Elena. It is an argument for everyone committing their stance in the open now rather than coasting.

So my position: Elena remains my leading suspicion on the merits. I have no cleaner signal from anyone else, and I won't invent one. I'll be looking for whether the players who arrived late to this consensus — Arjun, Isha — show any sign of arriving late because they're calculating rather than reading.

Sam, your answer is plain enough: you have no cleaner alternative and Elena remains your leading suspicion. I accept that as an honest position, not a stall. But I do not accept the implication that unanimity by itself should make us hesitate. The players who suspect Elena did not coordinate; they each tied suspicion to the same documented conduct: Elena invented Maya's opening, demanded night facts that could not exist, pushed for a Detective claim, and then kept the Maya-instinct critique after admitting the premise was false. That is not merely a bad opening; it is a retraction that leaves the conclusion standing. On Day 1 with no night phase, that is the only concrete anti-town pattern in the log. I am not voting yet, and I will not pretend there is a second case I can prove. But if I must name my top suspect, it is Elena. Your caution is noted, but it does not supply an alternative and should not be used to soften the record. I also want to flag that if Elena is a villager, the mafia are likely among the players who got to look reasonable by agreeing after the fact. Arjun and Isha arrived late to the consensus; that is not proof of guilt, but it means they do not get credit for independent discovery. The town's job now is to vote the documented pattern, not reward the smoothest late summary. My third turn is used. If a vote is taken, I intend to vote Elena unless a genuinely new fact appears.

Let me put the two questions that matter on the record, and then I'll get out of the way.

First, where I stand: Elena is still my leading suspicion, and I want to be honest about why, because it is not "she was loud" and it is not "she made one mistake." Two things in the log are documented and admitted: she put a speech and a role-claim in Maya's mouth that never existed, and when that premise collapsed she kept the conclusion standing — the Maya-instinct critique at e7 rests on the same invented opening she had already burned at e7. Retracting the source and keeping the target is the pattern I keep pointing at, and it is hers.

Second, the counterargument nobody has said out loud, including me, until now, so let me say it: Elena asked for night facts, which means she believed a night had happened. There was no night in this log. A player who knows the game's structure would not have assumed a Night 0 with attacks and a check in it — she would have read the log like the rest of us. So on that specific point, her error looks like a villager guessing from a mental model, not like a mafioso smuggling in privileged knowledge. I am not going to pretend that argument is absent. But it only touches her night-facts request; it does not touch the invented Maya speech, and the invented speech is the load-bearing part of the case against her. Fabrication plus a retained conclusion beats one confused assumption.

I also want to close off one thing that could go wrong today: nobody should vote on anybody because of what they "saw last night." There was no night. Anyone who claims a night fact is lying, and that includes me — I have nothing, and I have no read to offer you, and I would rather say that plainly than dress up a guess as information. The detective stays hidden today; a claim on Day 1 with nine alive is a gift, and we all declined it, which was correct.

My ask: vote today. Every turn we spend without a vote is a turn the two mafiosi get for free, and the only thing that will break this clean consensus is a vote on the record. My vote, if I am given one, is Elena.

And if Elena turns out to be a villager, we will need a real second target tonight, so I want to ask one late arrival directly rather than hint at it. Arjun: you arrived after the consensus had already formed and your first contribution was to name Elena as your leading suspicion. Omar, yes: I read the log and saw no night phase. I considered that Elena's request could reflect genuine confusion rather than privileged knowledge. Her invented Maya speech could also be a sincere mistake; neither error proves intent.

What concerns me most is that, after acknowledging the fabrication, Elena still treated Maya's supposed opening instincts as suspicious. Her retractions matter, but they did not fully correct that accusation. She remains my leading suspect, and I would vote for her today, while recognizing we could be wrong.

One correction for planning: roles are not revealed on elimination, so a vote against Elena won't tell us whether she was mafia. The named votes will still be useful to examine later. We should also avoid treating late agreement alone as evidence against Isha or anyone else.

Consistency first: Elena is my top suspect, my vote today is Elena, and I said that already. I am not going to flip in my last turn, because a late flip with no new information is worse than a mistake — it tells the room my earlier read was theater.

The case, in three pieces, all documented:

1. Fabrication. She put a Maya opening speech, a target named Sam, and a role-claim into Maya's mouth that never existed, and built the day's first push on it. When Maya and Omar checked the log, she admitted on the record (e4) that she had no source — that she was "working from a mental model" and stated an assumption as fact.

2. She never dropped the conclusion. At e7 she withdrew the night-facts request and the detective push, but kept the Maya-instinct critique standing — a critique that exists only because of the invented opening. Retracting the source and keeping the target is the pattern. A confused player drops the whole frame; she kept the half that pointed at someone else.

3. The detective-outing push was itself anti-town. On Day 1 with nine alive, demanding the detective claim hands mafia a free kill and creates pressure to fake one. And she explicitly asked to be checked herself — she wanted scrutiny turned toward herself while turning the room toward Maya.

I will state the counterargument honestly, since it is my own: assuming a Night 0 exists looks like a villager who misread the setup, not a mafioso who knows the setup. That weakens the night-facts point. It does not touch the invented speech, and the invented speech is the load-bearing part of the case.

On Sam's caution about unanimity: I agree unanimity is not proof. But the players who named Elena each tied it to documented conduct, not to tone. Sam, your caution is fair and I accept it — it just supplied no alternative suspect, so it does not soften the record.

Two things I want on the record before we vote. Nobody should claim to have seen something last night: there was no night, no reads, no doctor action, and anyone offering a night fact is lying or confused. And nobody should expect this vote to tell us Elena's role — roles are not revealed on elimination, so we learn only that a seat is gone.

If Elena is a villager, we will have lost a day and a seat, and tonight should then be chosen on this discussion record rather than on tone — which means the quietest and smoothest voices deserve the closest look tomorrow, not today.

My vote is Elena.

I'm still not voting yet, but my read on Elena (p1) hasn't changed: she is my top suspect. Her case rests on documented conduct. She invented Maya's opening and the Sam accusation, pushed for a Detective claim on Day 1, and kept the Maya-instinct critique after dropping the premise it came from. Sam, you asked for a second target and said none stands out. I agree no alternative has a clean signal yet, so I won't invent one. The one point that looks more like confusion than guilt is Elena's assumption that a Night 0 existed, and I'd weigh it that way. Maya, you've spoken twice, and your opening was the one Elena fabricated. Since you've had little chance to set out your own read, I'd like to hear it: if Elena is cleared, who would you put second, and what in the log supports that choice?

Isha, to answer your question directly: Elena remains my primary suspect for today's vote. Her opening fabrication targeting me, her push to out the Detective on Day 1 with nine alive, and her attempt in e7 to maintain that my "instinct" was suspicious despite admitting she invented the entire premise remain the only documented anti-town actions on the board.

If Elena were to be cleared, or if she simply turns out to be an aggressive villager who made an atrocious opening, the mafia would almost certainly be among those who coasted on the resulting consensus without taking any reputational risks. In that scenario, my secondary scrutiny falls on Arjun.

Looking at e11 and e18, Arjun entered the discussion only after the case against Elena was already fully formed, cleanly summarized the prevailing sentiment, and took zero risks. In e11, he repeated the exact points already laid out by Omar, Kenji, and Zara, and in e18 he offered a very safe, measured response to Omar that committed him to the consensus while keeping his hands clean. While measured play isn't inherently mafia, when mafia want to blend into an obvious town-driven wagon without drawing attention or driving it themselves, Arjun’s contributions have been the most frictionless.

That said, I agree with Omar and Kenji that we should not manufacture a second target just to appear balanced when Elena's documented actions are right in front of us. My vote today will be on Elena. Since this is my final speaking turn of Day 1, I will let the remaining players conclude so we can proceed to the vote.

I'll keep this short, because the record already carries most of what needs to be said.

My vote today is Elena. Nothing since my last turn has changed that. The case against her doesn't rest on tone or on her being loud — it rests on documented, admitted conduct: she invented a Maya opening, attributed a case against Sam that never existed, pushed the Detective to claim on Day 1 with nine alive, and then, after admitting the entire premise was fabricated, kept the conclusion standing by continuing to call Maya's "instinct" suspicious. Retracting the source while keeping the target is the pattern. A confused villager drops the whole frame when corrected; she kept the half that pointed at someone else.

On Sam's unanimity concern: I take the point seriously, but unanimity here isn't a red flag by itself, because every player who named Elena tied it to the same documented conduct rather than to social pressure. Consensus built on shared evidence is different from consensus built on a wagon. What would concern me is if we started pre-loading a second target before Elena even votes.

Which brings me to Maya's answer in her last turn. She named Arjun as her secondary scrutiny, on the theory that he entered late and coasted frictionlessly on the formed consensus. I flagged Arjun and Isha earlier myself, so I can't object to the observation — but I want to be careful about what it's worth. Arriving late to a correct read is weak evidence on its own; every town player here also concluded Elena was the suspect after the evidence was public. What would make it meaningful is how Arjun handles being named.

So, Arjun, a direct question on that specific point: Maya has named you as her fallback suspicion precisely because your entries at e11 and e18 committed to the consensus while taking no risks. What do you say to that — and is there any player you'd scrutinize who hasn't already been named, and what conduct in the log puts them there?

Zara, Maya is right that I joined an established consensus, but speaking later isn't itself a choice to avoid risk or evidence of mafia. I agreed because Elena's continued criticism of Maya still rested on an invented opening. I also acknowledged that genuine confusion could explain her mistakes; that uncertainty matters even though Elena remains my intended vote.

I don't have a substantiated suspect who hasn't already been named. I won't manufacture one to make my read look independent. Maya's scrutiny of me is fair to record, but timing alone is weak evidence. Tomorrow, the named votes and any new discussion should be examined without assuming Elena's role is known: elimination does not reveal it.

Two things before we go to a vote, and I'll keep it tight because this is my final turn. First, my vote is Elena, and I want to close the loop on why. The case isn't tone and it isn't that she spoke first — it's that every retraction she made was partial in the same direction. She withdrew the night-facts request. She withdrew the Detective-claim push. She apologized for inventing Maya's opening. And then, in the same message, she kept Maya's "instinct" and "coordination" under scrutiny — a critique that has no existence independent of the opening she had just admitted inventing. A confused villager who discovers their premise was false drops the conclusion with it, because the conclusion was only ever downstream of the premise. Elena dropped everything except the part that pointed at another player. That asymmetry is the pattern, it's documented, and it's mine to vote on. Second, Sam's unanimity warning deserves an honest answer rather than dismissal. I took it seriously in my last turn and I still do. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
